title: What do Victorian disability workers need for registration, the Code of Conduct and CPD?
description: Victoria's disability worker scheme: voluntary registration, the 10 hour CPD standard, the Code of Conduct for all workers and mandatory notifications.
shortAnswer: In Victoria, every disability worker must comply with the Disability Service Safeguards Code of Conduct and report notifiable conduct by other workers, whether or not they are registered. Registration with the Victorian Disability Worker Commission is voluntary and currently free. Registered workers renew each year on September 30 and must meet three registration standards in effect since October 1, 2025, including at least 10 hours of continuing professional development each registration year.
keyTakeaways: The Disability Service Safeguards Act 2018 (Vic) applies the Code of Conduct and mandatory notifications to all disability workers in Victoria, however their services are funded.
Registration is voluntary, free for the 2025 to 2026 and 2026 to 2027 periods, runs from October 1 to September 30, and must be renewed every year.
The CPD standard requires at least 10 hours each registration year, pro rata in the first year, with records kept for 2 years and audits possible.
Workers and employers must notify the Commission as soon as practicable of four kinds of notifiable conduct, and the Commission must consider a notification within 60 days.
The Commissioner can issue Prohibition Orders against unregistered workers, including interim orders of up to 12 weeks.
regulator: Victorian Disability Worker Commission and the Disability Worker Registration Board of Victoria
appliesTo: All disability workers in Victoria, including supervisors and managers of disability workers, regardless of funding source
Employers of disability workers, for mandatory notifications
Registered disability support workers and registered disability practitioners

sections.heading: How does Victoria's Disability Worker Regulation Scheme work?

blocks.text: The scheme has two layers: duties that bind every disability worker in Victoria, and a voluntary registration layer with professional standards. Both come from the Disability Service Safeguards Act 2018 (Vic), which sets out the functions of the Victorian Disability Worker Commissioner, the Victorian Disability Worker Commission (VDWC) and the Disability Worker Registration Board of Victoria. This page states the position as at November 2026.

The Act defines a disability worker as someone who provides a service to a person with disability, delivers it personally or supervises or manages another person who does, provides a service involving more than incidental contact, and whose service mainly aims to care for, treat or support a person with disability. Unpaid family members and private volunteers are excluded unless they work on behalf of an organization ([disability worker registration](https://www.vdwc.vic.gov.au/disability-worker-registration)).

The scheme sits alongside, not instead of, national rules. A worker at a registered NDIS provider still needs an [NDIS Worker Screening Check](/regulations/ndis-worker-screening-requirements) for a risk assessed role and still falls under the [NDIS Code of Conduct](/regulations/ndis-code-of-conduct-and-worker-orientation). The VDWC describes registration as an additional check that assesses skills, experience and commitment to CPD.

sections.heading: What does the Victorian Code of Conduct require of disability workers?

blocks.text: All disability workers in Victoria are legally required to comply with the Disability Service Safeguards Code of Conduct, which the VDWC says has the same requirements as the NDIS Code of Conduct ([Code of Conduct](https://www.vdwc.vic.gov.au/rights-and-responsibilities/disability-worker-code-of-conduct)). That covers respecting rights and privacy, providing supports safely and competently with care and skill, acting with integrity, raising concerns promptly, preventing and responding to violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation and sexual misconduct, and fair pricing of goods for NDIS participants.

The practical effect is reach. A worker funded through a state program, a private arrangement or the NDIS is held to identical conduct duties, so a provider operating across funding streams can use one Code of Conduct induction for its Victorian workforce. Registered workers are also bound to the Code through a Board guideline, on top of other registration responsibilities.

When the VDWC enforces the Code it considers the services delivered, the organizational environment, the worker's skills and qualifications, the person's support needs and other applicable regulation. Outcomes range from counseling and education, agreements and conciliation for complaints, referral to the NDIS Commission or Victoria Police, to investigation.

sections.heading: What must workers and employers report to the VDWC?

blocks.text: Disability workers and their employers must notify the VDWC as soon as practicable if they form a reasonable belief that another disability worker has engaged in notifiable conduct ([mandatory notifications](https://www.vdwc.vic.gov.au/notifications)). This is a duty for every worker, so it belongs in induction for all staff, not only registered ones.

items: **Intoxication** by alcohol or drugs, including prescription medicines, while practicing.
**Sexual misconduct** toward a person with disability, at any time including outside work hours.
**Impairment** that places, or may place, the public at risk because it detrimentally affects the worker's capacity to practice.
**Significant departure from accepted professional standards**, which include the Code of Conduct, that places the public at substantial risk of harm.

blocks.text: Reasonable belief needs direct knowledge or a report from a reliable source, more than suspicion but not certainty. A person with disability who directly employs a worker is exempt, and a worker need not notify if they know the notification has already been made. The VDWC must consider a notification within 60 days, and a notifier acting in good faith is protected from liability. A worker who fails to notify when required may face health, conduct or performance action.

sections.heading: Who can register and what does registration require?

blocks.text: Registration is open to anyone providing a disability service in Victoria, including supervisors and managers, and is currently free and voluntary. Registered workers appear on a public register, the registration year runs from October 1 to September 30, and renewal opens in early August and closes on September 30 ([for registered workers](https://www.vdwc.vic.gov.au/registered-workers)). The Board lists no fees for applications, renewals or late renewals for the 2025 to 2026 and 2026 to 2027 periods.

Applicants register as a disability support worker or a disability practitioner, on qualifications, experience or both, and everyone needs some disability work experience ([eligibility for registration](https://www.vdwc.vic.gov.au/eligibility-registration)). Applicants prove identity and agree to a national police check, which can be skipped by quoting a current NDIS Worker Screening ID.

blocks.caption: Registration pathways for disability support workers (VDWC eligibility criteria)
head: Pathway
Qualification requirement
Experience requirement
rows: Certificate III or higher in Individual Support, Disability, Aged Care Work or a related field, or equivalent training
Relevant disability work experience in the past 10 years (placement hours can count)
At least 1,440 hours over at least 2 years in the past 10 years
Qualification in community services, health or a related field relevant to the experience
At least 120 hours in the past 10 years

blocks.text: Disability practitioners follow parallel routes, with a Diploma or higher in a relevant professional discipline and professional registration where the profession requires it. The criminal history standard assesses history using the same decision making framework as the Worker Screening Act 2020, and the English language standard sets a minimum of Vocational English.

sections.heading: What does the CPD registration standard require?

blocks.text: Registered disability workers must complete at least 10 hours of CPD each registration year, under the Board's [CPD registration standard](https://www.vdwc.vic.gov.au/registration-standards/CPD) effective October 1, 2025. It is one of three registration standards (criminal history, English language and CPD) that took effect that day after a 2025 public consultation ([registration standards](https://www.vdwc.vic.gov.au/registration-standards)). Workers with non-practicing registration are exempt.

items: **Content:** activities must aim to improve outcomes for people with disability, build existing knowledge and skills in the worker's type of disability work, use up to date information where possible, and keep the worker current on policy, regulation and practice standards.

**Pro rata first year:** 2.5 hours for every 3 months of registration remaining, so 10 hours if registered October to December, 7.5 hours January to March, 5 hours April to June, and 2.5 hours July to September.

**What counts:** online modules, employer provided disability practice training, webinars and conferences, accredited course units, communities of practice, formal mentoring, technical reading, relevant committees, and some repeat or annual refresher training such as first aid. CPD done for another regulator, such as Ahpra, can count if relevant.

**Records:** a log of each activity's name, provider, date, location and hours, with reflection on how it improved practice, kept for 2 years after the registration period. The Board may audit declarations.

**Consequences:** if the standard is not met and no exemption was granted, the Board may renew subject to a condition or refuse renewal. Exemptions in exceptional circumstances can be full or partial, prorated by the months affected.

blocks.text: For employers, the useful detail is that employer delivered disability practice training counts toward a registered worker's 10 hours. A provider that issues certificates naming the activity, provider, date and hours makes its staff's renewal declarations easy to support. See [continuing professional development](/glossary/continuing-professional-development) for the general concept.

blocks.text: Providers working with children should add the [Working with Children Check](/regulations/working-with-children-check-requirements) and Victoria's [Child Safe Standards](/regulations/victoria-child-safe-standards-training), which apply separately.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry can map a provider's disability practice training to the CPD standard's four content criteria, so each module records which criterion it serves and how many hours it represents. That gives registered workers evidence for their declarations and gives the provider a view of Code and notification training across both registered and unregistered staff.

faqs.q: Is disability worker registration compulsory in Victoria?
faqs.a: No. Registration with the Victorian Disability Worker Commission is voluntary and currently free. The Code of Conduct and mandatory notification duties apply to every disability worker in Victoria regardless of registration, and the Commissioner can issue Prohibition Orders against unregistered workers who pose a serious risk.

faqs.q: Can CPD hours from my employer's training count toward registration?
faqs.a: Yes. The CPD standard accepts disability practice training provided by your employer, along with online modules, webinars, accredited units, mentoring and some refresher training such as first aid, provided the activity is relevant to your disability practice. Record the name, provider, date, location and hours of each activity.

faqs.q: What happens if a registered disability worker does not complete 10 hours of CPD?
faqs.a: Unless the Board granted an exemption, it may renew the registration subject to a condition or refuse to renew it. The Board will invite the worker to respond to the proposal before deciding. Exemptions are available for exceptional circumstances such as significant illness, prolonged caring responsibilities or bereavement.

faqs.q: How long does an interim Prohibition Order last?
faqs.a: The VDWC states that orders may be permanent or for a limited period of up to 12 weeks, which is called an interim prohibition order. Orders can be revoked, amended or carry conditions. They apply to unregistered disability workers and stop the person from providing all or specified disability services in Victoria.

Three registration standards (criminal history, English language, CPD) took effect 1 October 2025 after 2025 consultation.

CPD standard: at least 10 hours per registration year; pro rata 2.5 hours per 3 months; non-practicing exempt; records kept 2 years after the registration period; Board may audit; may renew with condition or refuse; standard made under Part 10, Division 1 of the Act.

Activities that count include employer provided training, online modules, refresher training such as first aid; CPD for Ahpra can count if relevant; renewal declaration requires activity name, provider, date, location and hours; exemption prorating.
All disability workers in Victoria are legally required to comply with the Code, which has the same requirements as the NDIS Code of Conduct; enforcement factors and outcomes.

Mandatory notifications: four categories (intoxication, sexual misconduct, impairment, significant departure); as soon as practicable; Commission must consider within 60 days; good faith protection; exemptions.

Support worker pathways: Certificate III with experience in past 10 years; 1,440 hours over at least 2 years in past 10 years; combination with 120 hours; NDIS Worker Screening ID avoids new police check.
Renewal opens early August and closes 30 September; registered workers abide by the Code via a Board guideline; no fees for 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 periods.
Prohibition Orders against unregistered disability workers; interim orders up to 12 weeks.
